transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21
Time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood Solutions); Lena (OpsGarden ML Ops), Rajiv (Platform), Marta (Security), Tom (SRE)

Summary (auto): OpsGarden exploring Redwood Dedicated for production inference. Primary drivers: tenant isolation, predictable latency for low-p99s, and burst handling during trading windows. Constraints include strict KMS/HSM usage, SOC2+ISO required, and desire for a hot-pool prewarm to keep cold-starts <250ms for core endpoints.

Topics: Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, reserved capacity sizing, isolation options (node/tenant pinning, MIG), burst model (prewarm, hot pools, gating), fallback to hosted, compliance/keys, next steps and benchmark plan.

Transcript body:
00:00:03 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro from my side: Maya Patel, AE at Redwood. Diego is our SE, he'll jump into the infra bits.
00:00:10 Lena: Hi all, Lena from OpsGarden. We're trying to map out how to move our inference traffic off the current self-host and into something that doesn't require 24/7 ops. We've been looking at Redwood hosted and dedicated.
00:00:25 Diego: Great, thanks. Can you give us a sense — what's the steady-state QPS and when do bursts happen?
00:00:33 Rajiv: Sure, steady is about 60 qps across three endpoints, peaks can hit 800 qps for short windows, maybe 3-7 minutes during market opens in 2 timezones. There's also long tails where we want lower latency for premium users.
00:00:50 Marta: Two quick constraints: all encryption must be customer-managed KMS, and audit logs retained for 7 years. Also we need SSO/SAML integration and RBAC.
00:01:04 Diego: Understood. Those map to our Private and Dedicated options — Dedicated supports VPC peering and customer KMS with our Private control plane pattern, and we can surface audit logs to your SIEM.
00:01:18 Tom: Is that the same as Redwood Private? I've seen some docs that call it Redwood Privet, sorry.
00:01:23 Hannah: (laughs) That's the pronunciation trap — Redwood Private is the private deployment. Dedicated is our reserved GPU pools hosted by Redwood but isolated at the tenant level.
00:01:35 Lena: Practically what isolation means for us is tenant pinning: certain models must never share GPUs with other customers. Does Redwood support that?
00:01:45 Diego: Yes. We can do node-level reservation and tenant fencing. For NVIDIA we use MIG partitions or full-GPU pinning based on the size of your model. There are tradeoffs — full-GPU gives strict isolation and consistent latency but costs more.
00:02:02 Rajiv: We also use heavy KV cache warm-ups for prefix reuse; any prewarming strategy to avoid cold KV reads?
00:02:10 Diego: We have a hot-pool concept — prewarmed instances that keep KV caches in memory and maintain kv pointers. For big models the KV warm-up can be several seconds otherwise. Hot-pool plus prefix caching reduces that to sub-200ms for many workloads.
00:02:30 Lena: Can hot-pool scale during burst? Say it goes from 60 to 800 qps in 2 minutes.
00:02:38 Diego: The burst model is multi-tier: 1) hot-pool of reserved prewarmed nodes; 2) autoscale within your Dedicated pool (reserved capacity + ephemeral extra nodes up to a configured burst cap); 3) automated fallback to smaller model variants or our hosted nodes if Dedicated is saturated.
00:02:56 Tom: Fallback to hosted — that has data residency implications for us. Will data leave our VPC?
00:03:04 Diego: Good question. For Dedicated we can route fallback to Redwood-hosted only if you opt into it; otherwise the fallback can be to a lower-capacity Dedicated variant or to a different region. We can also encrypt traffic with your KMS so keys never leave your control, but full on-prem data residency would point to Private deployment.
00:03:24 Marta: For compliance, we need HSM-backed keys and proof of key separation. Is KMS integration with HSM an option?
00:03:31 Maya: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations with attestation. I'll link our security whitepaper in the follow-up.
00:03:38 Rajiv: One architecture concern — NUMA boundaries and PCIe fabric in multi-GPU nodes. We see variance in p99 depending on model size and whether a request crosses GPU boundaries. Do you have recommended node profiles?
00:03:50 Diego: For that we recommend homogeneous full-GPU nodes for latency-critical endpoints to avoid cross-GPU hops. For batch-like endpoints we can use multi-GPU with MPS or quantized kernels. We'll share kernel profiles and sample NUMA mappings.
00:04:10 Lena: What's the billing model when we have reserved nodes + burst ephemeral? Is burst charged at different rates?
00:04:16 Maya: Reserved capacity is a committed monthly rate with a utilization credit; ephemerals are metered at a higher per-minute rate. We also have a blended model if you commit to a larger reserved buffer. Diego, do you have a sample cost model?
00:04:28 Diego: I'll run three scenarios: conservative (50 tps peak), moderate (200 tps peak), aggressive (500+ tps bursts) with expected token mixes. I'll include prewarm hours cost and hot-pool sizing.
00:04:39 Marta: We need latency SLOs — specifically p95 < 120ms and p99 < 350ms for premium endpoints. Can Redwood meet this with Dedicated?
00:04:48 Diego: Yes for most models if you do full-GPU pinning and hot-pool. p99 gets trickier with cold starts and KV cache. That's why we recommend prewarm policies per endpoint.
00:05:05 Rajiv: Are model variants allowed — like fall back to a smaller quantized variant during bursts? We have quality tolerance for some endpoints.
00:05:12 Diego: Absolutely. We support traffic rules to fallback to quantized variants or earlier model versions. You can do weighted traffic splitting and canary rollouts through our Console.
00:05:25 Lena: We are worried about noisy neighbors inside Dedicated pools — other tenants generating burst traffic. How strict is tenant fencing?
00:05:34 Diego: With node-level pinning and isolated pools you eliminate noisy neighbor risk. The tradeoff is utilization. We can also use tenant shaping and request queues to limit impact.
00:05:45 Tom: What's the expected time to scale ephemerals? If hot-pool is exhausted, how long until new nodes are healthy?
00:05:52 Diego: Ephemeral provisioning can be ~60-180s depending on region and image preload. Hot-pool is for the <60s ramp; ephemeral is the next layer. For very low-latency needs we recommend a larger hot-pool or warm standby nodes.
00:06:10 Marta: Logging: we need token-level audit traces and per-request latency histograms exported to our ELK/Splunk. Can that be done without sending PII?
00:06:19 Hannah: We can export anonymized traces and also field-level redaction. We'll provide logging controls.
00:06:30 Lena: Great. Let's talk scale expectations. We plan to onboard 4 more endpoints by Q3, with a 3x increase in average qps. How do we capacity plan?
00:06:39 Maya: We typically size two ways: model-profile-driven (profile your warm seq length and tokens) and traffic-driven (peak qps). We'll do both in the cost model Diego prepares. For Q3 expansion we can propose a staged reservation plan.
00:06:56 Rajiv: Do you support preemptible lower-cost nodes for non-critical batch workloads?
00:07:02 Diego: Yes, we offer preemptible/gpu spot-like nodes for background batch with lower SLAs and lower cost; not for premium endpoints.
00:07:12 Lena: How is canary deploy handled when we change model weights? We need an automatic rollback when quality drops.
00:07:20 Hannah: Our Console supports canaries with metrics-based rollback rules tied to eval sets. If perplexity or custom evals regress, you can auto rollback. We also have manual controls.
00:07:34 Tom: We might need a short performance test that simulates your market open bursts. Can Redwood run benchmarks in our account?
00:07:41 Maya: Yes, we can run a benchmark run in a staging Dedicated pool or inside your VPC Private deployment. We'll need a test plan and traffic replay.
00:07:50 Rajiv: Any gotchas on quantization? We run some models on q4_0; previously we've seen quality regressions.
00:07:57 Diego: We'll include recommended quantization profiles by model family. Some workloads are sensitive; we'll call those out and recommend hybrid approaches.
00:08:08 Lena: How often do you do kernel swaps/updates that could change latency characteristics?
00:08:14 Diego: We have a change window and a canary cadence; kernel updates are staged and customers on Dedicated can opt into faster or more conservative tracks.
00:08:24 Marta: For audit, we want a paper trail of kernel/cfg changes and their deployment windows — is that available?
00:08:30 Hannah: Yes, we provide deployment artifacts and changelogs; for enterprise customers we can extend retention.
00:08:36 Maya: Quick recap — folks, I want to summarize next steps: Diego will produce cost/burst scenarios, I'll send pricing and security notes, and we schedule a deep technical session. Any objections?
00:08:48 Lena: Sounds good. One more question — do you do scheduled prewarm before predictable events? We have daily market opens at 09:30 and 16:00 UTC.
00:08:58 Diego: Yes, you can schedule prewarm jobs or use predictive prewarm based on historical patterns. We can also do rule-based triggers tied to upstream signals.
00:09:10 Rajiv: Ok that's helpful. On fallback we want to avoid sending sensitive request bodies to hosted fallback — how do we ensure that?
00:09:18 Diego: You can configure data handling policies per route; hosted fallback requires explicit opt-in and only anonymized contexts are sent; otherwise fallback must stay within Dedicated/Private.
00:09:30 Marta: We'll review the SSO/SAML and KMS docs. Please include sequence diagrams for key flows.
00:09:37 Maya: Will do.
00:09:42 (background) Speaker overlap / minor crosstalk
00:09:50 Lena: thanks everyone.
